candidates.title: External sandboxes for coding agents
candidates.author: Simon Willison
candidates.organization: Simon Willison's Weblog (work done with Prime Radiant)
candidates.what_changed: Simon and Prime Radiant introduce the 'external sandbox' pattern and release three open-source sandbox server implementations that coding agents (Pi, Claude Code, Codex) can call to execute code.
candidates.mechanism: The agent process lives outside the sandbox; only code it wants to execute is sent over a common localhost API to a dedicated sandbox server. Three back ends share the same API: external-sandbox-v86 (Node.js server running Alpine Linux in WebAssembly via v86), external-sandbox-container (Python server, Alpine in Apple Containers), external-sandbox-quicksand (Python server using Microsoft's Quicksand library, which bundles QEMU + Alpine in a Python package). Optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy controls which hosts executed code can reach, reconfigurable live via a UI; a credential-replacement mechanism lets sandboxed code make authenticated API calls without the secret ever being shared with the agent.
candidates.evidence_quality: Practitioner link-post describing released code; no benchmarks or threat-model evaluation. The fuller write-up is on the Prime Radiant blog (blog.primeradiant.com) which could NOT be fetched (egress proxy 403), and GitHub repo pages returned HTTP 403, so repo details (licence, setup steps, API shape) are UNVERIFIED.
candidates.independent_confirmation: Latent Space AI News (Nov 17) summarises the post (allow-list proxies, credential replacement, WASM/QEMU/Apple Container) but cites Simon's post, so not independent.
candidates.relevance: HIGH. Directly tryable this week: point your coding agent's execution at a sandbox server, restrict egress with an allow-list, keep secrets out of the agent's context. Especially useful for running local/open-weight models with less trust.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Related to Edition 1's security theme ('if the limit lives in the prompt, the agent will find the way around it'): this is a concrete enforcement-layer implementation (network allow-list + credential injection outside the agent), so it is materially new as a how-to, but should be framed as a follow-up rather than a repeat.
candidates.summary: Simon Willison has been exploring ways to sandbox code executed by agents, focusing on making it safer to try local models without a mistake or prompt-injection attack causing damaging actions on the host. With Prime Radiant (the lab behind Superpowers) he introduces the external sandbox pattern: the agent runs outside, and any code it wants to run is sent to a separate sandbox. Three implementations with an identical localhost API: (1) external-sandbox-v86 — Node.js server using v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly; (2) external-sandbox-container — Python web server running Alpine in an Apple Containers instance; (3) external-sandbox-quicksand — Python web server using Microsoft's Quicksand, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a pip-installable package. Pi, Claude Code or Codex can be configured to send API calls to the sandbox whenever they want to execute code. Optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy lets you control exactly which hosts the agent's code can talk to, reconfigurable while the sandbox is running via a UI; a credential replacement mechanism lets code make authenticated calls without sharing the secret with the agent (same idea as proxy-side secret injection). Repos: github.com/prime-radiant-inc/external-sandbox-v86, -container, -quicksand (links from post; contents UNVERIFIED, GitHub returned 403). Primary write-up: https://blog.primeradiant.com/external-sandboxes-for-coding-agents/ (UNVERIFIED, blocked).

candidates.title: Running the full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers and Pyodide
candidates.author: Simon Willison
candidates.what_changed: Complete rewrite of Datasette Lite using service workers; now nearly indistinguishable from server-side Datasette, with URL params to pick Datasette version/commit, SQLite version, plugins. New repo of WASM pysqlite3 wheels for many SQLite versions.
candidates.mechanism: Service worker registered for lite.datasette.io intercepts requests from an iframe to /app/<session-id>/... URLs; random per-tab session ID routes each request back through the parent page to a dedicated Pyodide web worker running that tab's Datasette instance (web worker needed because Pyodide in a service worker can't keep state beyond ~30s). URL params: ?install= (PyPI plugins/wheels, repeatable), &url= (DB, needs open CORS; Gists used), &metadata=, ?ref= (release/commit/tag/branch), ?sqlite=3.54.1 (fetches matching wheel from datasette/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels and installs it), #fragment for in-app location.
candidates.evidence_quality: First-hand project write-up with working demo URLs. Minor internal inconsistency on page: says 'over 100 versions of SQLite', '87 further releases since 3.25', and wheels for '163 different SQLite versions'.
candidates.independent_confirmation: None (newsletter subtitle on Simon's own Substack echoes it).
candidates.relevance: MEDIUM. AI angle: system started as an AI research spike generated with Claude Opus 4.8 in May, shipped only after Claude Fable 5.2 helped him understand it; Claude Fable 5.2 generated SVG diagrams and a SQLite version-comparison tool. Practical pattern: WASM/Pyodide preview environments for bug repros and demos in PRs; coding agents can now compile C/Rust extensions to Pyodide WASM (PEP 783, April 2026 allows publishing to PyPI).
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Edition 1 cited datasette-maplibre (Nov 15) — this post uses datasette-maplibre as its demo. Distinct item but adjacent; avoid re-covering the plugin.
candidates.summary: Datasette Lite (launched 2022) previously ran Datasette in a Pyodide web worker and injected HTML via innerHTML, so script tags didn't execute and JS/CSS plugins failed. The rewrite uses Service Workers: the parent page creates an iframe whose requests go to /app/<session>/ prefixed URLs; the shared service worker uses the session ID to route each request back via the parent page to a dedicated web worker running Datasette for that tab, so multiple tabs with different plugin configurations don't share one instance. Features: load any SQLite DB, JSON, CSV or SQL script by URL; pick Datasette release from PyPI or a GitHub commit/tag/branch (?ref=); install plugins from PyPI or wheel URLs incl. JS visualization plugins; pick SQLite version (?sqlite=). Use case: linking demos of WIP features and bug reproductions in issues, e.g. a pagination bug shown with ?ref=1.0a42 (broken) vs ?ref=1.0a43 (fixed). New repo datasette/pysqlite3-wasm-wheels holds WASM pysqlite3 wheels for 163 SQLite versions (e.g. pysqlite3-0.6.2-3.54.1-cp314-cp314-pyemscripten_2026_0_wasm32.whl); Claude Fable 5.2 built a tool to compare a SQL query across SQLite versions. Simon argues almost any Python app could do this as cheap preview environments; coding agents can compile C/Rust extensions to Pyodide-compatible WASM, publishable to PyPI per PEP 783 (April 2026). Catch: Postgres/MySQL in WASM still less trodden.

candidates.title: llm 0.37.3
candidates.author: Simon Willison
candidates.pub_date: 2026-11-16 (11:57 pm per Simon's Nov 16 day archive https://simonwillison.net/2026/Nov/16/; GitHub release page not fetched, returned 403 for GitHub generally)
candidates.what_changed: Bug-fix release of LLM addressing breakage in logging code caused by SQLite 3.54.1 (shipped in Homebrew).
candidates.mechanism: In SQLite 3.54.0, select json_object('a', (select json_array(1))) returned {"a":[1]}; in 3.54.1 it returns {"a":"[1]"}. D. Richard Hipp: 3.54.1 is correct, a subquery returning json_array returns SQL text, not JSON. Workaround: wrap with json(): select json_object('a', json((select json_array(1)))).
candidates.evidence_quality: First-hand maintainer note with quoted SQLite author; reproducible SQL.
candidates.independent_confirmation: Simon's Datasette Lite post includes a tool demonstrating the same difference between 3.54.0 and 3.54.1. SQLite release log link not fetched (UNVERIFIED).
candidates.relevance: MEDIUM-LOW as a brief: anyone storing LLM/agent logs as JSON in SQLite (nested json_object/json_array subqueries) may see silently stringified JSON after upgrading to SQLite 3.54.1; fix is to wrap with json().
candidates.summary: Posted in Simon's 'Release' feed on 16 Nov at 11:57 pm (after Edition 1 went out). Homebrew now ships SQLite 3.54.1, which fixed a bug in 3.54.0 that LLM's logging code had relied on: nested (SELECT json_array(...)) inside json_object now yields a string rather than embedded JSON. Fix: json((select json_array(1))). Tracking issue https://github.com/simonw/llm/issues/1879 (UNVERIFIED, not fetched). Good one-paragraph brief for anyone with SQLite-backed telemetry.

candidates.title: Cloudflare Joins the Jevolution and Labels Itself a Neolab
candidates.author: Richard MacManus
candidates.event_date: Talk at AI Engineer Code Summit (date not stated on page, UNVERIFIED) plus post-talk interview with Michelle Chen
candidates.what_changed: Cloudflare's AI Platform product lead says Cloudflare is now building its own models: two 'System One' models, Clef (a decision model cloning TypeSafe AI's Jev, built in two weeks) and Clairic (a 'System One extraction model'), with possible post-trained reasoning models/LLMs later.
candidates.mechanism: System One models route some requests away from LLMs to small fast models answering in milliseconds. Clairic takes unstructured input and extracts/computes/estimates/forecasts typed values (e.g. an invoice's order number) in one forward pass, avoiding autoregressive hallucination and malformed JSON. Team mostly does post-training, not from-scratch pretraining. Rationale includes derisking dependence on closed or license/regulation-risky third-party models.
candidates.evidence_quality: Reported interview/talk; vendor claims, no benchmarks or accuracy numbers for Clef/Clairic on the page. Revenue figures quoted from Cloudflare Q3 press release ($782M quarter, $3B annualized, +39% YoY).
candidates.independent_confirmation: Clairic launch blog linked (https://blog.cloudflare.com/clairic-extraction-model/, not fetched, UNVERIFIED).
candidates.relevance: MEDIUM. Applied takeaway: for structured extraction (invoices, typed fields) and decisions, consider a small dedicated extraction/decision model on Workers AI instead of an LLM call, for latency and reliability. Needs evals before adoption.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Edition 1 Operations theme (routing to the right model / cheaper model) is adjacent; Cloudflare was cited in Ed 1 for security/spend posts but not this.
candidates.summary: Michelle Chen (Cloudflare AI Platform, product) presented at AI Engineer Code Summit that Cloudflare is a 'neolab'. It launched two System One models: Clef, a decision model directly inspired by and copying the API schema of TypeSafe AI's Jev (Chen: two weeks to build vs TypeSafe's two years, credit to TypeSafe), and Clairic, launched last month as 'the first model in a new class: System One extraction models' that takes unstructured input and extracts, computes, estimates and forecasts values. Motivation: 'We don't have to send every request to an LLM'; LLMs are autoregressive, hallucinate and sometimes return malformed JSON; invoice order-number example. Plans: possibly reasoning models and other LLMs built by post-training existing open models, not pre-training. Also derisking: Jev was closed source, Chinese open models may face regulatory risk, labs may enforce expensive licences. Cloudflare progression: infra -> compute (Workers, incl. agents) -> storage -> serving open-weight models (Kimi, GLM, DeepSeek on Workers AI) -> own models. Neolab definition attributed to Stephanie Palazzolo (The Information); Deedy Das list.

candidates.title: Building Visual Intelligence — Andreas Blattmann & Dustin Podell, Black Forest Labs
candidates.author: swyx (host); guests Andreas Blattmann, Dustin Podell

candidates.what_changed: Podcast with BFL on FLUX 3 (trained jointly on stills, video and audio), video upscaler derived from the FLUX 3 backbone, Kontext editing, autoregression vs diffusion trade-offs.
candidates.mechanism: Training on image + video + audio together: video teaches motion and multi-view appearance (camera pans), audio marks contact events. Per-frame upscaling shimmers on playback; BFL's video upscaler is derived from the FLUX 3 backbone for temporal consistency. Autoregressive models learn from all tokens in an example at once; diffusion can be distilled to a handful of sampling steps — choose by whether you pay training or inference latency. Kontext began as a few-hour training run on a small relationship-labelled photo set.
candidates.evidence_quality: Interview; qualitative claims, no numbers in show notes.
candidates.relevance: LOW-MEDIUM for this audience (image/video gen practitioners). Usable nuggets: test video features on temporal consistency, not single-frame quality; prototype capability with a few-hours small-data run before investing.
candidates.summary: swyx talks with Andreas Blattmann (co-creator of Stable Diffusion/latent diffusion) and Dustin Podell (led FLUX Kontext, lead author SDXL). BFL argues for learning 'visual intelligence' from pixels, motion and sound: ball-catching example; FLUX 3 trained on the three signals together. A camera panning around a person forces the model to produce the back of their head — a better test than whether one frame looks convincing. Engineering example: independently sharpened frames shimmer on playback; BFL derives its video upscaler from FLUX 3 for temporal consistency. Autoregression vs diffusion trade-off discussed. Kontext origin: small labelled photo set, a few-hour run got logo-on-shirt editing working, then months on data and model. User story: restoring degraded family photos. Chapters include training data, testing an edit, world action models, robotics in 2027.

candidates.title: Pre-Training Without Learning Rate Decay
candidates.author: Sebastian Raschka
candidates.what_changed: Raschka flags a possible trend: pre-training with a constant learning rate and no decay phase, plus averaging the last N checkpoints (or a running weight average), as in Kolibri-1 and DatologyAI's models.
candidates.mechanism: Constant LR + checkpoint/weight averaging replaces cosine decay or warmup-stable-decay; practical upside is not having to commit to total training length upfront.
candidates.evidence_quality: Short note (website version of an X post) with a meta-tally of published recipes; no new experiments.
candidates.independent_confirmation: Cites DatologyAI's note on weight averaging; Latent Space AI News Nov 17 mentions DatologyAI's tech report (6x pretraining compute multiplier claim, UNVERIFIED).
candidates.relevance: LOW-MEDIUM: relevant to teams doing continued pre-training or training small models; you can stop/extend runs without re-planning the schedule and average checkpoints for the final weights.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Edition 1 research corner cited Raschka's positional embeddings article (Nov 15); this is a different topic.
candidates.summary: Three schedule families tallied from labs that share training details: classic cosine decay (Llama 3, OLMo 2, OLMo 3, GLM-4.5, GLM-5, Kimi K3, Phi-4); WSD warmup-stable-decay (DeepSeek V3, V4, V4.1-Flash, Kimi K2, Kimi Linear, Nemotron 3 Nano, Nemotron 3 Super, SmolLM3, MiniMax M2); no decay, constant LR plus checkpoint averaging (Kolibri-1, DatologyAI's models). Raschka: 'This could be the start of a trend'; easier in practice because you don't commit to total training length upfront. Includes a figure comparing the three schedules.

candidates.title: Deterministic Simulation Testing
candidates.author: Unmesh Joshi
candidates.pub_date: 2026-11-17 (confirmed on page; recent-changes lists Tue 17 Nov 2026 09:33 EST)
candidates.what_changed: Long-form article on deterministic simulation testing (DST) for distributed systems with Tickloom (Java) code, including a section on using LLMs with a DST harness.
candidates.mechanism: Replace clocks, network and storage with simulated components driven by a single-threaded tick loop; seeded fault injection (partitions, link delays/drops, disk latency) makes every run reproducible (same seed -> same faults -> same results); fast-forward execution; ConsistencyChecker verifies linearizability/crash durability. AI angle: tick-stamped fault schedule + execution logs are 'particularly effective when handed to an LLM to analyze what went wrong'; with the harness in place an LLM can translate a book diagram (DDIA quorum linearizability anomaly) into an executable scenario test (DDIA_LinearizabilityScenarioTest).
candidates.evidence_quality: Expert practitioner article with code; LLM claims are qualitative experience, no measurements.
candidates.independent_confirmation: References TigerBeetle, FoundationDB, etcd practices; reviewed by Martin Fowler, Rebecca Parsons, Will Wilson, Joran Dirk Greef.
candidates.relevance: LOW-MEDIUM for AI audience: mainly distributed-systems testing. Applied AI hook: deterministic, seeded harnesses + structured logs give LLMs/coding agents reproducible failures to diagnose and a safe place to generate scenario tests; fits 'verification for agents' angle.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Loosely adjacent to Ed 1's 'let a rule grade what the agent did' (deterministic checkers as fitness functions).
candidates.summary: Distributed bugs live in interactions under partial failure ('gray failures'). DST: single-threaded execution, simulated network with message routing, timeouts in ticks (TigerBeetle tick_ms=10; etcd 100ms ticker, 10-tick election timeout), seeded fault injection, fast-forward execution, correctness checking, simulated file system, non-blocking futures. Determinism rules enforced via ArchUnit static checks plus runtime thread-confinement (TickCompletableFuture rejects calls from non-owner threads). Seeded FaultInjectingSimulationRunner + ConsistencyChecker act as a holistic fitness function. Production cost: single-threaded async batched IO often performs better (Redis, FoundationDB, TigerBeetle); scale via multiple processes. Section 'Learning and the Use of LLMs': harness lets LLMs act as natural-language interface to build/explore systems; LLM generates executable scenario tests from textbook diagrams; tick-stamped logs ideal for LLM diagnosis.
